summary: This document describes a proxy mechanism that allows IPv6 nodes to use Duplicate Address Detection in point-to-multipoint networks with split-horizon forwarding, mainly DSL and fiber access. The first-hop router keeps a binding table of known addresses and responds when a node tries an address already in use by another.

eli5.summary: When someone picks a house number, a helper checks the list and says "taken!" if another neighbor already has it, even when neighbors cannot hear each other.

questions: duplicate address detection in split-horizon networks
why does ipv6 dad not work with split horizon
what is a binding table in ipv6
how does a bng defend an ipv6 address
subtitle: How a first-hop router can defend IPv6 addresses when hosts on the same network cannot hear each other.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Duplicate Address Detection relies on every node on a link hearing the others, but in DSL and fiber networks with a split-horizon scheme the customer devices can only talk to the first-hop router.
tldr.mechanism: The first-hop router (BNG) records every address it sees in a Binding Table. When a device tries an address already bound to another device, the router checks that the first device is still reachable and, if so, answers the newcomer with a Neighbor Advertisement.
tldr.outcome: Only the first-hop router needs changing, not the other IPv6 nodes. The RFC is clear that the result is not completely reliable and does not fix DAD itself.

today: RFC 6957 is a Proposed Standard from June 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says the mechanism is not completely reliable because it is based on DAD.

sections.title: The DAD Proxy in Brief
sections.content:
RFC 6957 specifies a function called the DAD proxy. It lets nodes on a point-to-multipoint domain with a split-horizon forwarding scheme use Duplicate Address Detection (DAD). That setup is primarily deployed for DSL and fiber access architectures. The proxy only affects the first-hop router; other IPv6 nodes need no modification.

The mechanism is fully effective only if all nodes in the domain, except the DAD proxy itself, perform DAD. The RFC also assumes link-layer addresses are unique from the first-hop router's point of view. In an untrusted Ethernet architecture, that can be guaranteed by something like MAC address translation in an aggregation device.
sections.eli5: Normally neighbors can shout to check if a house number is taken. Here the neighbors are behind walls, so a helper in the middle has to do the checking for them.

sections.title: The DSL and Fiber Setting
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. The CPE (Customer Premises Equipment) is the first IPv6 node in a customer's network. The Access Node (AN) is the first aggregation point in the public access network, treated as an L2 bridge. The BNG (Broadband Network Gateway) is the first-hop router from the CPE's point of view. In a VLAN N:1 architecture, many CPEs share one VLAN.

In the split-horizon model, CPEs cannot communicate directly at layer 2. Their traffic must be forwarded through the BNG by routing. So the BNG is on the same link as every CPE, but no CPE is on the same link as another CPE.
sections.eli5: Every house has a private road that leads only to the town hall. Houses never see each other, but the town hall sees every house.

sections.title: Why Existing Solutions Fall Short
sections.content:
Standard DAD (RFC 4862) has a node send a Neighbor Solicitation (NS) to the solicited-node multicast address of its tentative address, and any current owner replies with a Neighbor Advertisement (NA). With split-horizon, an NS from one CPE reaches only the BNG, so other CPEs never learn that an address is in use.

The RFC walks through alternatives and why each does not fit:

  • ND Proxy (RFC 4389): on the AN it would forward to the BNG only; on the BNG it cannot be used, because the BNG must not forward link-local scoped messages from one CPE to others.
  • 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery (RFC 6775): needs changes in all hosts to support the Address Registration Option.
  • Mobile IPv6 home agent (RFC 6275): the home agent multicasts NAs on the link, but access operators require that an NA be received only by the sender of the NS, for security and scalability.
sections.eli5: Other fixes either need every kid to learn new rules, or they tell everyone every secret. This one only changes what the teacher does.

sections.title: The Binding Table
sections.content:
The BNG keeps a Binding Table per point-to-multipoint domain, such as per Ethernet VLAN. It can be separate from the Neighbor Cache. Each entry MUST contain an IPv6 address and a link-layer address. For security or performance, it must be possible to limit the number of IPv6 addresses per link-layer address, possibly to 1.

If an unsolicited NA arrives for an address already in the table, such as when a CPE announces a new link-layer address, every entry for that address MUST be updated with the new link-layer address.

The table MUST be large enough for its deployment, and at least as large as the Neighbor Cache if the two are distinct. Implementations MUST state their fixed table size, or their maximum size if it is configurable, and SHOULD let an operator check how full the table is. A full table will likely be handled like NS message loss.
sections.eli5: The teacher keeps a notebook with two columns: the nickname and which kid owns it. The notebook must be big enough for the class.

sections.title: How the BNG Handles a DAD Message
sections.content:
A CPE doing DAD sends an NS with the unspecified address as its source. The BNG acts on it based on the Binding Table.

No entry exists. The BNG MUST create an entry with the tentative address and the link-layer source address of the NS. It MUST NOT reply or forward the NS.

An entry exists. If the link-layer source matches the entry, the same CPE is still doing DAD, and the BNG again MUST NOT reply or forward. If it differs, another CPE may be trying an address already owned, so the BNG MUST check whether the conflict is real, depending on the Neighbor Cache:

  • Address cached with the same link-layer address: confirm reachability with Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD).
  • Address cached with a different link-layer address: out of scope, since the RFC assumes all nodes perform DAD.
  • Address not cached: the BNG MUST create a cache entry in the STALE state from the Binding Table entry, then confirm reachability as soon as possible.
sections.eli5: If the nickname is new, the teacher writes it down and stays quiet. If the same kid asks again, still quiet. If a different kid asks for a taken name, the teacher first checks whether the first kid is still in class.

sections.title: Confirming the Conflict and Replying
sections.content:
Reachability is checked with NUD from RFC 4861, triggered as though a packet had to be sent to the existing owner. In some cases, such as a recently confirmed REACHABLE entry, NUD does nothing.

If NUD is negative, the old owner is gone, so the conflict is not real. The old Binding Table entry is deleted and replaced with one for the new CPE's link-layer address.

If NUD is positive, the conflict is real, and the BNG MUST reply to the CPE doing DAD with an NA. That NA is addressed at layer 2 to the asking CPE, goes to the all-nodes multicast address at the IPv6 level, and carries the already-used address as its Target Address. The BNG and the CPE MUST support unicast transmission at the link layer of IPv6 multicast messages (RFC 6085), so they can send and process such a packet.
sections.eli5: Before saying taken, the teacher calls out to the first kid. No answer means the name is free again. An answer means the second kid hears taken, and must pick another.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
The BNG SHOULD log and raise alarms when it detects address duplication, and SHOULD let an operator read the logs and the current Binding Table. Access rights for this are out of scope.

The mechanism does not interoperate with SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND, RFC 3971), because the BNG does not hold the private key of the Cryptographically Generated Address needed to sign proxied ND messages. Secure Proxy ND Support for SEND (RFC 6496) addresses this and SHOULD be implemented and used on the BNG and the CPEs.

For protection against IP source address spoofing in data packets, the proposal can be combined with Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) mechanisms. If so, the BNG is the SAVI device and a CPE's MAC address is its Binding Anchor.
sections.eli5: The teacher should write down every naming clash and let the principal read the list. The special secret-handshake system for kids needs extra rules, because the teacher cannot sign for them.
